butir.teks: It is the same with the knowledge of unveiling ('ilm al-mukashafa), the secrets of the knowledge of conduct ('ilm al-mu'amala), and the subtle points of the passing thoughts of the heart. Each of these branches of knowledge is a sea whose depth cannot be reached; each seeker plunges into it only as far as he has been provided with it and according to the good conduct he has been granted success in. In describing these scholars, Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said in a long hadith: “Hearts are vessels, and the best of them is the one that holds the most good. People are of three kinds: a divine scholar (rabbani), a learner on the path of deliverance, and the riffraff and rabble, followers of every caller, who sway with every wind. They have not sought light
by the light of knowledge, and have not taken refuge in a firm pillar. Knowledge is better than wealth: knowledge guards you, while you guard wealth.

Knowledge grows through spending, while wealth is diminished by spending. Knowledge is a religion that is followed; through it obedience is gained during one's life and a fair reputation after one's death. Knowledge is the judge and wealth is judged. The benefit of wealth ends when it ends. The keepers of wealth die while they are alive, while the scholars live on as long as time remains. Then he sighed deeply and said: “Ah! Here indeed is abundant knowledge, if only I could find bearers for it! Instead I find a seeker who is not trustworthy, using the instrument of religion to seek this world, lording it over Allah's friends with Allah's favours, and relying on his argument against His creation; or one who submits to the people of truth, but doubt is planted in his heart by the first doubtful argument that comes up, with no insight, neither this one nor that; or one ravenous for pleasures, easily led in pursuing appetites, or devoted to amassing wealth and hoarding it, led by his caprice (hawa). The grazing cattle are the closest in likeness to them. O Allah! Thus knowledge dies when its bearers die. Yet the earth is never without one who stands for Allah with a proof, either manifest and known or fearful and overpowered, so that Allah's proofs and clear signs do not come to nothing. How many are they, and where? They are the fewest in number and the greatest in standing. Their persons are missing, but their likenesses are present in hearts. Through them Allah Most High preserves His proofs until they entrust them to those after them and plant them in the hearts of their like. Knowledge has come upon them with the reality of the matter, so they have touched the spirit of certainty, finding easy what the pampered found rough, and feeling intimacy with what the heedless found desolate. They have accompanied this world with bodies whose spirits are attached to the highest place. Those are the friends of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, among His creation, His trustees, His agents in His earth, and the callers to His religion.” Then he wept and said: “How I long to see them!” This last thing he mentioned is the description of the scholars of the Hereafter, and it is the knowledge most of which is gained from action and persistent spiritual struggle (mujahada).

Among these is that he is very concerned with strengthening certainty (yaqin), for certainty is the capital of religion. The Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) said: “Certainty is faith in its entirety.” (١) So one must learn the knowledge of certainty, I mean its beginnings; then its path opens up for the heart. For that reason he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: “Learn certainty.” (٢) Its meaning is: sit with those who have certainty, listen to them teach the knowledge of certainty, and keep following their example, so that your certainty may grow strong as theirs grew strong. A little certainty is better than much action.

He (peace and blessings be upon him) said, when it was said to him that there is a man of excellent certainty with many sins, and a man who strives in worship but has little certainty, the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: “There is no son of Adam without sins, but whoever's innate nature is intellect and whose disposition is certainty, sins do not harm him, because whenever he sins he repents, asks forgiveness, and feels regret, so his sins are expiated and a surplus remains to him by which he enters Paradise.” (٣) For that reason he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: “Among the least of what you have been given are certainty and the resolve of patience; whoever is given his share of both does not care what he misses of night prayer and daytime fasting.” (٤) In the counsel of Luqman to his son: “My son, action cannot be done except with certainty; a person acts only according to his certainty; and a worker does not fall short until his certainty diminishes.” Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: “Tawhid has a light and shirk has a fire, and the light of tawhid burns up the evil deeds of those who affirm Divine oneness more than the fire of shirk burns up the good deeds of the polytheists.” By this he meant certainty. Allah Most High has indicated in the Qur'an the mention of those who have certainty in several places, by which He showed that certainty is the bond of good things and of felicities.

If you say, “What is the meaning of certainty, and what is the meaning of its strength and weakness?”, it must first be understood, and only then pursued by seeking and learning it, for what you do not understand the form of cannot be sought. Know that certainty is a shared term that two groups apply to two different meanings. As for the speculative thinkers (nuzzar) and the theologians (mutakallimun), they express by it the absence of doubt, since the soul's inclination toward affirming something has four stations (maqamat). The first: affirmation and denial are equal, and this is expressed as doubt, as when you are asked about

a particular individual, whether Allah Most High will punish him or not, while his state is unknown to you. Your soul does not incline to judge about him either by affirmation or by negation; rather the possibility of the two matters is equal for you. This is called doubt (shakk).

The second: your soul inclines to one of the two matters while being aware of the possibility of its opposite, but a possibility that does not prevent the first from being preferred, as when you are asked about a man you know to be righteous and God-conscious, whether he in particular would be punished if he died in this state. Your soul inclines more to the view that he would not be punished than to punishment, because the signs of righteousness are apparent.

Yet along with this, you allow that something deserving punishment is hidden in his inner self and his secret. This allowance is on a par with that inclination, but it does not repel its preponderance. This state is called conjecture (zann).

The third: the soul inclines to affirming something such that it predominates in it and nothing else crosses the mind, and if something else did cross the mind, the soul would refuse to accept it; but that is not accompanied by verified knowledge, for if the holder of this station were to reflect well and listen to the casting of doubt and allowance, his soul would open to the allowance. This is called belief (i'tiqad) close to certainty, and it is the belief of the common people in all matters of the Sharia, since it took root in their souls through mere hearing, so much so that every group is confident of the soundness of its school and of the rightness of its imam and the one it follows, and if the possibility of its imam's error were mentioned to any of them, he would recoil from accepting it.

The fourth: true knowledge obtained by way of demonstration about which there is no doubt and about which doubt cannot be conceived. When the existence of doubt and its possibility are impossible, it is called certainty (yaqin) according to these people. An example: if an intelligent person is asked, “Is there anything in existence that is eternal (qadim)?”, he cannot affirm it by self-evident intuition, because the eternal is not perceptible, unlike the sun and the moon, whose existence he affirms by sense perception. And knowledge that there exists an eternal, beginningless thing is not necessary like the knowledge that two is more than one, and like the knowledge that the coming into being of a thing without a cause is impossible, for this too is necessary. So it is the due of the innate nature of the intellect to withhold affirming the existence of the eternal on the spur of the moment and by self-evidence. Then among people there are those who hear that and affirm it by hearing with firm affirmation and remain constant in it. That is belief (i'tiqad), and it is the state of all the common people.

And among people are those who affirm it by demonstration, which is that it is said to him: if there is no eternal thing in existence, then all existing things are originated; if all are originated, then they are originated without a cause, or something among them is originated without a cause, and that is impossible; and what leads to the impossible is impossible. So the intellect is bound to affirm of necessity the existence of an eternal thing, because the divisions are three: that all existing things are eternal, or all are originated, or some are eternal and some originated. If all are eternal, then the goal is achieved, since an eternal thing has been established in general. If all are originated, that is impossible, since it leads to origination without a cause. So the third division or the first is established.

Every piece of knowledge obtained in this way is called certainty according to these people, whether it is obtained by speculation such as what we have mentioned, or by sense perception, or by the innate nature of the intellect such as knowledge of the impossibility of something originated without a cause, or by mass transmission (tawatur) such as knowledge of the existence of Mecca, or by experience such as knowing that boiled scammony is a purgative, or by proof as we mentioned. The condition for applying this name according to them is the absence of doubt, so every piece of knowledge without doubt in it is called certainty by them. On this basis certainty is not described as weak, as there is no variation in the negation of doubt.

The second usage is the usage of the jurists, the Sufis, and most scholars. It does not look in this to the consideration of allowance and doubt, but rather to its dominance and prevailing over the intellect, so that it is said, “So-and-so is weak in certainty of death,” even though there is no doubt in it, and it is said, “So-and-so is strong in certainty about the coming of provision,” though it is possible that it will not come to him. So whenever the soul inclines to affirming something and this prevails over the heart and gains mastery until it becomes the one governing and directing the soul by allowing and forbidding, that is called certainty. There is no doubt that people share in being sure of death and in being free of doubt about it, but among them are those who pay no attention to it nor to preparation for it, as though he were not certain of it.

And among them are those in whose heart this takes hold so that it absorbs all his concern in preparing for it and leaves no room in it for anything else; such a state is expressed as strength of certainty. For that reason one of them said: “I have never seen a certainty with no doubt in it more like a doubt with no certainty in it than

death.” In this usage certainty is described as weak and strong. By our saying that it is characteristic of the scholars of the Hereafter to direct their concern to strengthening certainty, we intended both meanings: the negation of doubt, and then giving certainty dominion over the soul so that it is the prevailing one, governing it and directing it.

When you have understood this, you know that what is meant by our saying that certainty is divided into three kinds is: by strength and weakness, by abundance and fewness, and by obscurity and clarity. As for strength and weakness, it is according to the second usage, and that lies in dominance and mastery over the heart. The degrees of the meanings of certainty in strength and weakness are unlimited, and people's differing in preparing for death is according to the differing of their certainty in these meanings. As for variation by obscurity and clarity in the first usage, it too is not denied. As for that which allowance can reach, it is not denied, I mean the second usage; and in that from which doubt has also been removed there is no way to deny it, for you perceive a difference between your affirming the existence of Mecca and of Fadak, for example, and your affirming the existence of Moses and Joshua (peace be upon them both), though you doubt neither. Their basis in both cases is mass transmission (tawatur), yet you see one of them clearer and more evident in your heart than the other, because the cause in one is stronger, namely the abundance of those reporting. Likewise the speculative thinker perceives this in the matters known by proofs: the clarity of what appears to him by one proof is not like the clarity of what appears to him by many proofs, though they are equal in negating doubt. This the theologian may deny, who takes knowledge from books and hearsay and does not consult himself about the variation of states he perceives.
As for fewness and abundance, that is by the abundance of what certainty relates to, as it is said, “So-and-so has more knowledge than so-and-so,” meaning his known things are more.

For that reason a scholar may be strong in certainty in everything the Law has brought, and he may be strong in certainty in some of it. If you say, “I have understood certainty and its strength, weakness, abundance, fewness, clarity, and obscurity, in the sense of negation of doubt or in the sense of mastery over the heart; so what is the meaning of the objects of certainty and its fields, and in what is certainty sought? For as long as I do not know what certainty is to be sought in, I cannot seek it,” know that everything the prophets (blessings and peace of Allah be upon them) brought, from its first to its last, belongs to the fields of certainty, for certainty is a particular knowledge, and its object is the known matters that the revealed laws brought. There is no hope of enumerating them, but I will point to some of them, which are their mothers. Among them is tawhid, which is that he sees all things as coming from the Causer of causes and pays no attention to the intermediaries, but sees the intermediaries as subjugated, with no ruling power of their own. The one who affirms this is a person of certainty. If the possibility of doubt is removed from his heart along with faith, then he has certainty in one of the two senses. If there prevails in his heart, along with faith, a dominance that removes from him anger at the intermediaries, pleasure with them, and thanks to them, and the intermediaries stand in his heart in the position of the pen and the hand in relation to the benefactor who bestows by signing, for he does not thank the pen or the hand nor become angry at them, but sees them as two subjugated instruments and two intermediaries, then he has become certain in the second sense, which is the overview (ishraf). It is the fruit of the first certainty, its spirit and its benefit.

Whenever he realises that the sun, the stars, inanimate things, plants, animals, and every creature are subjugated by His command, like the subjugation of the pen in the hand of the writer, and that the eternal power is the source of all, there prevails over his heart the dominance of reliance (tawakkul), contentment, and submission, and he becomes certain, free of anger, rancour, envy, and bad character. This is one of the gates of certainty.

Among these is trust in Allah's guarantee of provision, in His saying, Most High, ⟦QS 11:6⟧, and certainty that it will come to him and that what is decreed for him will be driven to him. Whenever that prevails in his heart, he is moderate in seeking, and his greed, his avidity, and his regret over what he has missed do not intensify, and this certainty also bears a number of acts of obedience and praiseworthy traits.

Among these is that there comes to prevail over his heart that ⟦QS 99:7-8⟧, which is certainty of reward and punishment, such that he sees the relation of acts of obedience to reward as the relation of bread to satiety, and the relation of acts of disobedience to punishment as the relation of poisons and vipers to destruction. Just as he is keen to obtain bread in order to be sated, so that he guards its little and its much, so he is keen on all acts of obedience, the little of them

and the much of them. And just as he avoids little of poisons and much, so he avoids acts of disobedience, their little and their much, small and great. Certainty in the first sense may be found among believers in general, but the second sense is specific to those brought near (muqarrabun). The fruit of this certainty is sincere vigilance (muraqaba) in movements and stillnesses and passing thoughts, going to the utmost in God-consciousness (taqwa), and guarding against all evil deeds. The stronger the certainty, the stricter the guarding and the more thorough the girding up.

Among these is certainty that Allah Most High is aware of you in every state and witnesses the whispers of your conscience and the hidden recesses of your passing thoughts and reflection. This is held with certainty by every believer in the first sense, which is the absence of doubt; but in the second sense, which is the intended one, it is rare and specific to the truthful ones (siddiqun). Its fruit is that a person in his solitude is well-mannered in all his states, like one sitting in the presence of a revered king who is looking at him: he does not cease to keep his head lowered and be well-mannered in all his actions, composed, guarding against every movement that goes against the form of proper conduct (adab). His inward thought is like his outward deeds, since he realises that Allah Most High is aware of his inner secret as creatures are aware of his outward appearance, so his striving to build up his inner being, purify it, and adorn it, under the eye of Allah Most High who is present, is stronger than his striving to adorn his outward appearance for the rest of people. This station of certainty yields modesty, fear, brokenness, abasement, submissiveness, and humility, and a number of praiseworthy traits, and these traits yield kinds of lofty acts of obedience. Certainty in each of these gates is like a tree; these traits in the heart are like the branches that spring from it; and these works and acts of obedience that issue from the traits are like the fruits and blossoms that spring from the branches. So certainty is the root and foundation, and it has more fields and gates than we have counted, and that will come in the Quarter of the Saving Traits (munjiyat), if Allah wills.
This much suffices for the meaning of the word for now.

Among these is that he is sorrowful, broken, head lowered, silent; the mark of awe shows in his appearance, his clothing, his conduct, his movement and stillness, his speech and silence. No onlooker looks at him without looking at him reminding him of Allah Most High, and his outward form is a proof of his work. The noble steed's eye is its mirror. The scholars of the Hereafter are known by their mark in tranquillity, abasement, and humility. It has been said: “Allah has not clothed a servant with a garment better than humility in tranquillity; it is the garment of the prophets, and the mark of the righteous, the truthful ones, and the scholars.” As for flightiness in speech, loquacious affectation, immersion in laughter, and sharpness in movement and speech, all of that is among the effects of insolent exuberance, feeling secure, and heedlessness of the great punishment of Allah Most High and His severe anger, and it is the habit of the sons of this world, who are heedless of Allah, not of those who know Him. This is because the scholars are three, as Sahl at-Tustari (may Allah have mercy on him) said: a scholar of the command of Allah Most High but not of the days of Allah, and they are the muftis in the lawful and the forbidden, and this knowledge does not yield awe; a scholar of Allah Most High but not of the command of Allah nor the days of Allah, and they are the believers in general; and a scholar of Allah Most High, of the command of Allah Most High, and of the days of Allah Most High, and they are the truthful ones (siddiqun), and awe and humility prevail over them. By the days of Allah he meant the kinds of His hidden punishments and inward favours that He poured upon the past and later generations. Whoever's knowledge encompasses that, his fear becomes great and his humility appears.

Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: “Learn knowledge, and learn for knowledge tranquillity, dignity, and forbearance. Be humble to those you learn from, and let those who learn from you be humble to you. Do not be among the tyrants of the scholars, for then your knowledge will not stand against your ignorance.”
It is said: “Allah never gives a servant knowledge without giving him along with it forbearance, humility, good character, and gentleness; that is beneficial knowledge.”
In a report (athar): “Whoever Allah has given knowledge, renunciation (zuhd), humility, and good character is the leader of the God-conscious.”

In the report (khabar): “Among the best of my community are people who laugh openly at the vastness of Allah's mercy and weep in secret from fear of His punishment; their bodies are on the earth and their hearts in heaven, their spirits in this world and their minds in the Hereafter; they walk with tranquillity and seek nearness through the means (wasila).” (١) Al-Hasan said: “Forbearance is the minister of knowledge, gentleness is its father, and humility is its garment.”
Bishr ibn al-Harith said: “Whoever seeks
leadership through knowledge, draw near to Allah Most High by hating him, for he is detested in heaven and on earth.”

It is related among the Israelite narratives that a sage composed three hundred and sixty works on wisdom, until he was described as a sage. Then Allah Most High revealed to their prophet: “Tell so-and-so: You have filled the earth with hypocrisy, and you have not wanted Me by any of it, and I accept nothing of your hypocrisy.” The man regretted and abandoned that, mixed with the common people in the markets, ate with the Children of Israel, and was humble within himself. Then Allah Most High revealed to their prophet: “Tell him: Now you have been granted success in My pleasure.”

Al-Awza'i (may Allah have mercy on him) related from Bilal ibn Sa'd that he used to say: “One of you looks at the policeman and seeks refuge in Allah from him, and looks at the scholars of this world who put on a show for people and crane toward leadership, and does not detest them, though they are more deserving of detestation than that policeman.”

It is narrated that it was said: “O Messenger of Allah, which deeds are best?” He said: “Avoiding the forbidden things, and that your mouth never ceases to be moist with the remembrance of Allah Most High.” It was said: “Which companions are best?” He (peace and blessings be upon him) said: “A companion who, if you remember Allah, helps you, and if you forget Him, reminds you.” It was said: “Which companions are worst?” He (peace and blessings be upon him) said: “A companion who, if you forget, does not remind you, and if you remember, does not help you.” It was said: “Which people are most knowledgeable?” He said: “Those who fear Allah most.” It was said: “Then tell us who are our best, that we may sit with them.” He (peace and blessings be upon him) said: “Those who, when seen, remind of Allah.” It was said: “Which people are worst?” He said: “O Allah, forgive!” They said: “Tell us, O Messenger of Allah.” He said: “The scholars when they become corrupt.” (١) He (peace and blessings be upon him) said: “The people with the most security on the Day of Resurrection are those who reflected most in this world; the people who laugh most in the Hereafter are those who wept most in this world; and the people who rejoice most in the Hereafter are those who grieved longest in this world.” (٢) Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said in a sermon of his: “My pledge is a hostage, and I stand guarantor for it that the crop of a people built on God-consciousness does not wither, and the root of a stock built on guidance does not go thirsty. The most ignorant of people is he who does not know his own worth, and the most hated of creation to Allah Most High is a man who has gathered scraps of knowledge, with which he ran headlong into the dim darkness of discord; those like him among people and the lowest of them call him a scholar, though he never spent a day safe in knowledge. He made much of himself and sought more, and what is little of it and sufficient is better than what is much and distracting, until, when he had drunk his fill of stagnant water and amassed much without benefit, he sat for the people as a teacher, to untangle what had become confused for others. If one of the important matters comes upon him, he prepares for it a stuffing of opinion from his own opinion. So he and whoever cuts through doubts are in something like a spider's weaving, not knowing whether he erred or was right; a rider of ignorances, one who stumbles in the dark. He does not excuse himself from what he does not know so as to be safe, nor does he bite into knowledge with a cutting molar so as to gain. Blood weeps because of him, and forbidden private parts are made lawful by his judgment. By Allah, he is not fit to dispatch what comes to him, nor is he worthy of what has been entrusted to him. Those are the ones upon whom exemplary punishments have fallen, and for whom wailing and weeping are due during the days of the life of this world.”
Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said: “When you hear knowledge, hold it in, and do not mix it with jest, lest hearts spit it out.”
One of the early generations (salaf) said: “A scholar, when he laughs a laugh, spits out of knowledge a mouthful.”
